verdict.rationale: Ghostty's docs describe a file-based configuration with hundreds of options. It can be split across multiple files via the `config-file` key, keybindings and themes are set as config lines, and community users share plain-text config snippets, so keeping the config as text in dotfiles is clearly supported at its core. Nothing documents the config file location, portability, or a supported cross-machine sync workflow, and default bindings differ by platform; syncing relies on the user's own dotfiles tooling. missing for 10: documented config file path/format details confirming the entire configuration lives in plain text, explicit guidance on portability or sync across machines (including handling of macOS/Linux differences), independent hands-on corroboration of a dotfiles-synced setup.

support.subject: As a power-user, I can keep the terminal's full configuration as plain-text files in my dotfiles and sync it across machines

citations.quote: Ghostty supports hundreds of configuration options to make it look and behave exactly how you want.
You can split your configuration into multiple files by using the `config-file` key in your configuration file.
Ghostty supports flexible, custom keybindings through the keybind configuration option.
Ghostty ships with hundreds of themes that can be selected with a single line of configuration.
To blend Ghostty in better with XFCE, add to config: window-theme = system, gtk-titlebar = false, gtk-wide-tabs = false, gtk-adwaita = false.
